Block Recursive Transformers for Structured Parameter Sharing

Josep Marques Affiliation: Sungkyunkwan University    Hyunyoung A. Cho Affiliation: Sungkyunkwan University    Youngeun Kim Affiliation: Korea University    Youjia Zhang Affiliation: Sungkyunkwan University    Aecheon Jung Affiliation: Sungkyunkwan University    Kyuhong Shim Affiliation: Sungkyunkwan University    Sungeun Hong
Abstract

Recursive Transformers depend not only on how many parameters are shared, but also on how shared parameters are organized across depth. Existing static schemes adopt two extreme reuse topologies: layer-wise repetition, where each layer is reused independently, and global cyclic reuse, where the entire stack is repeatedly applied as a single shared function. We argue that sharing granularity is an important factor in recursive parameter sharing. This study proposes Block Recursive Transformers (BRT), which partition layers into contiguous blocks and recursively reuse each block before moving to the next. This intermediate topology enables local refinement within blocks while preserving depth-wise transitions, without adding routing modules, auxiliary states, or extra training objectives. Across decoder-only models up to 1.7B parameters, with additional encoder-decoder and encoder-only studies, BRT improves validation negative log-likelihood and downstream accuracy over static recursive sharing baselines. Ablations and representation analyses further show that intermediate block granularity better balances local refinement and depth-wise differentiation. Project website: https://aim-skku.github.io/BRT/

22footnotetext: Corresponding author: Sungeun Hong (csehong@skku.edu)

1 Introduction

Recursive Transformers reduce the number of unique model parameters by reusing layers while preserving the executed depth of the network (Shen et al., 2022; Bae et al., 2025a; Geiping et al., 2025). This makes parameter sharing attractive for compact language models, where the goal is to retain the benefits of deep computation while reducing the number of unique trainable layers.

Existing static sharing strategies follow two extreme reuse topologies. Sequence sharing repeats each layer independently before moving to the next,

as in Sequence-style assignment and intra-layer recurrence (Takase and Kiyono, 2023; Nguyen and Lin, 2025). This preserves a notion of depth, but treats each layer as a separate reuse unit, making it difficult to reuse multi-layer transformations as a coherent stage. In contrast, Cycle sharing repeatedly applies the shared stack as a single global function, as in cyclic or recursive reuse schemes (Takase and Kiyono, 2023; Bae et al., 2025a; Bae et al., 2025b; Yu et al., 2026). This improves downstream performance, but forces the same transformation to serve all depth-specific roles, which can cause redundant updates and representational saturation (Yu et al., 2026). Other compact language model designs use layer sharing for efficient generation (Liu et al., 2024; Reid et al., 2021), but do not explicitly study recursive reuse topology as the main design axis. As illustrated in Figure 1, Sequence and Cycle sharing form two boundary cases: overly fine-grained reuse and overly global reuse.

This raises the central question of this work: How should shared parameters be organized across depth? Transformer depth is not a homogeneous sequence of interchangeable layers. Prior analyses suggest that layers at different depths often play specialized functional roles (Liu, 2025; Sun et al., 2025; Shim et al., 2022). For example, lower layers tend to preserve more local and lexical information, while upper layers integrate higher-level features and become more closely tied to prediction behavior (Zhang et al., 2024). This motivates a reuse unit that is larger than a single layer, so that local transformations can be reused as a coherent stage, but smaller than the entire network, so that different depth regions can remain distinct.

In this study, we introduce Block Recursive Transformers (BRT), a recursive sharing architecture that partitions depth into contiguous blocks and recursively reuses each block before moving to the next. This intermediate topology enables local refinement, repeated application of a short multi-layer transformation within the same depth region, while preserving transitions across depth. We add no routing modules (Bae et al., 2025b; Yu et al., 2026), auxiliary memory states (Yu et al., 2026), layer-wise adaptation modules (Bae et al., 2025a), or extra training objectives. By only changing how shared layers are organized and executed, BRT isolates reuse topology as the main variable within a unified static sharing framework.

Our method improves downstream accuracy and validation negative log-likelihood over static recursive sharing baselines, and ablations and representation analyses support the benefit of intermediate block granularity. Rather than adding adaptive mechanisms, BRT isolates how static shared layers should be organized across depth, treating reuse topology as the main design axis for comparing Sequence, Cycle, and block-level reuse within a unified framework.

Our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We formulate static recursive parameter sharing as a reuse-topology problem and introduce Block Recursive Transformers (BRT), which recursively reuse contiguous groups of layers.

  • •

    We show that Sequence and Cycle sharing are boundary cases of the same block-wise formulation, enabling controlled comparison across reuse granularities without routing modules, auxiliary states, or extra objectives.

  • •

    We evaluate BRT across decoder-only model sizes, data budgets, and recursion settings, with additional encoder-decoder and encoder-only validation-NLL studies. BRT improves over static recursive sharing baselines with fewer unique trainable parameters.

2 Related Work

Cross-layer Parameter Sharing.

Parameter sharing has been widely studied as a way to reduce the number of unique parameters in Transformers. Early approaches impose strong tying across depth. Universal Transformers apply the same transformation recurrently across layers (Dehghani et al., 2019), while ALBERT shares parameters across Transformer layers to reduce memory usage (Lan et al., 2020). Although effective for compression, reusing a single layer can limit the representational capacity of different depth regions.

Recent approaches relax this constraint by sharing some components or adding layer-specific capacity. Subformer combines middle-layer sharing with embedding factorization for generative Transformers (Reid et al., 2021), and EdgeFormer augments shared layers with layer-specific adaptation for efficient on-device generation (Ge et al., 2022). MobileLLM uses layer sharing for compact sub-billion language models (Liu et al., 2024), while Basis Sharing decomposes layer weights into shared bases and layer-specific coefficients (Wang et al., 2025). Overall, these methods mainly study which parameters are shared or how sharing constraints are relaxed. In contrast, BRT studies how shared parameters are reused after they are tied. It keeps the layer parameterization unchanged, but reorganizes execution by grouping adjacent layers into recursive blocks. This shifts the focus from parameter tying itself to the topology of reuse across depth.

Recursive and Adaptive-depth Transformers.

Recursive Transformers construct depth by repeatedly applying shared layers, making parameter reuse an explicit iterative computation mechanism. Relaxed Recursive Transformers improve this idea with layer-wise LoRA adaptation (Bae et al., 2025a), while recurrent-depth models study repeated latent computation for test-time scaling (Geiping et al., 2025). Related looped Transformer studies further show that repeated computation can support iterative refinement and algorithmic behavior (Yang et al., 2024; Giannou et al., 2023; Fan et al., 2025; Gatmiry et al., 2024). Most static recursive sharing schemes, however, rely on either layer-wise repetition or a single global loop, corresponding to Sequence and Cycle sharing strategies (Takase and Kiyono, 2023). These topologies are parameter-efficient, but they either fragment reuse into individual layers or force a single shared stack to serve all depth-specific roles.

Recent adaptive-depth methods introduce mechanisms to decide how much computation each token should receive. Mixture-of-Recursions learns token-level recursive depths through routing (Bae et al., 2025b), while MeSH introduces a routing mechanism to support recursive computation (Yu et al., 2026). Unlike these methods, which change the amount or path of computation through routing, memory states, or adaptive schedules, we keep the computation schedule fixed and change only the granularity of reuse. This makes BRT a controlled setting for studying reuse topology and an orthogonal complement to routing- or memory-based recursive models.

3 Block Recursive Transformers

3.1 Reuse Granularity Analysis

BRT treats reuse granularity as a controllable design axis. Instead of reusing individual layers or the full stack, it recursively reuses contiguous groups of layers, reflecting the observation that Transformer layers often form depth-dependent functional groups rather than a uniform stack of interchangeable transformations (Geva et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024).

To examine how different reuse topologies affect depth-wise representations, we use Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) (Kornblith et al., 2019) as a diagnostic tool. CKA measures the similarity between hidden-state representations, allowing us to compare how representations evolve across layers and recursion steps. Importantly, CKA is not used to choose block boundaries. Instead, BRT adopts a fixed contiguous partition, so that the number of blocks directly controls reuse granularity and can be evaluated through ablations.

Figure 2 shows the resulting CKA patterns. The vanilla Transformer exhibits gradual representation changes across depth, suggesting that adjacent layers often form locally coherent stages. Sequence sharing shows high similarity across layers, indicating limited depth-wise differentiation when each layer is reused independently. Cycle sharing shows high similarity across recursion steps, consistent with representational saturation under global reuse (Yu et al., 2026). In contrast, BRT shows higher similarity within each block and lower similarity across blocks. This pattern supports the view that block-level reuse enables local refinement within each depth region while preserving transitions between different regions. Additional CKA visualizations are provided in Appendix B.

3.2 Formulation

We start from a standard LL-layer Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), whose hidden states are updated as:

hℓ=ℬ⁡(hℓ−1,θℓ),ℓ∈[1,L],h^{\ell}=\mathcal{B}\left(h^{\ell-1};\theta_{\ell}\right),\qquad\ell\in[1,L], (1)

where h0h^{0} is obtained from the token embedding, ℬ\mathcal{B} denotes a Transformer block, and θℓ\theta_{\ell} denotes the parameters of layer ℓ\ell.

Block Reuse.

Given a target executed depth LL, let EE denote the number of non-recursive boundary layers and RR the recursion count. Following prior recursive Transformer settings (Bae et al., 2025a; Bae et al., 2025b), the recurrent core contains P=(L−E)/RP=(L-E)/R unique recurrent layers when exact depth matching is feasible. The total number of unique layers is then T=P+ET=P+E, and the executed depth is L=P⋅R+EL=P\cdot R+E.

We partition the PP unique recurrent layers into SS contiguous blocks, where 1≤S≤P1\leq S\leq P. For clarity, we first describe the case where PP is divisible by SS, so each block contains K=P/SK=P/S layers. When this divisibility condition is not satisfied, we use the closest feasible contiguous partition: we choose the largest recurrent-core size P′≤PP^{\prime}\leq P such that P′P^{\prime} is divisible by SS, set K=P′/SK=P^{\prime}/S, and use Dexec=P′​R+ED_{\mathrm{exec}}=P^{\prime}R+E as the executed depth. This rule keeps block sizes equal, preserves contiguity, and never gives BRT a larger executed depth than the target vanilla model. We report the resulting executed depth for all configurations in Appendix A.

For block ss, we define its computation as:

ℱs=ℬ(⋅;θs,K)∘⋯∘ℬ(⋅;θs,1),\mathcal{F}_{s}=\mathcal{B}(\cdot;\theta_{s,K})\circ\cdots\circ\mathcal{B}(\cdot;\theta_{s,1}), (2)

where θs,1,…,θs,K\theta_{s,1},\ldots,\theta_{s,K} are the parameters of the KK layers in block ss. The composition follows the original layer order within each block, matching the forward execution order of a standard Transformer.

The block count SS controls the granularity of reuse. As SS increases, each reuse unit becomes smaller and the topology approaches layer-wise repetition. When S=1S=1, the recurrent core becomes a single global loop. Intermediate values 1<S<P1<S<P define BRT. In this regime, each block is applied RR times before representations move to the next block, enabling local refinement within contiguous layer groups while preserving transitions across depth.

Design Rationale.

We use contiguous blocks to keep recursive refinement local while allowing different depth regions to remain distinct. Thus, block-level reuse provides an intermediate topology between layer-wise repetition and global cyclic reuse.

By default, we set E=2E=2, keeping the first and last layers independent of the recursive core, following prior work (Bae et al., 2025b). The overall computation is then:

hout=ℬ(ℱSR(⋯ℱ1R(ℬ(h0;θ1)));θL),h_{\text{out}}=\mathcal{B}\!\left(\mathcal{F}_{S}^{R}\Big(\cdots\mathcal{F}_{1}^{R}(\mathcal{B}(h^{0};\theta_{1}))\Big);\theta_{L}\right), (3)

where ℱsR\mathcal{F}_{s}^{R} denotes RR repetitions of block ℱs\mathcal{F}_{s}, and θ1,θL\theta_{1},\theta_{L} denote the independent boundary layers.

Unifying Static Sharing Topologies.

With SS controlling reuse granularity and EE controlling boundary-layer sharing, prior static strategies arise as boundary cases.

  • •

    S=1S=1 gives global cyclic reuse, where the recurrent core is reused as one block. With E=0E=0, this recovers Cycle sharing; with E=2E=2, it corresponds to Middle-Cycle sharing.

  • •

    S=PS=P gives layer-wise repetition, where each recurrent layer is repeated before moving to the next. With E=0E=0, this recovers Sequence sharing; with E=2E=2, it corresponds to Middle-Sequence sharing.

  • •

    Intermediate values 1<S<P1<S<P define BRT, interpolating between these extremes through block-level recursive reuse.

4 Experiments

We evaluate BRT to answer three questions: (i) whether block-level reuse improves over static recursive sharing baselines under matched training budgets, (ii) whether the gains persist across model scale, data scale, and recursion depth, and (iii) whether the same reuse topology transfers beyond decoder-only architectures.

4.1 Experimental Setup

We use LLaMA-based SmolLM models up to 1.7B parameters (Touvron et al., 2023; Allal et al., 2024), pretrained from scratch on FineWeb-Edu (Penedo et al., 2024). We evaluate ARC, WinoGrande, MMLU, HellaSwag, and PIQA using the Language Model Evaluation Harness (Sutawika et al., 2024), and report mean performance across three seeds. We further evaluate encoder-decoder T5-220M and encoder-only ModernBERT-149M (Raffel et al., 2020; Warner et al., 2025). For language-modeling quality, we compute validation negative log-likelihood on 2,000 FineWeb-Edu samples.

Unless otherwise stated, recursive variants are compared under the same recursion count and training-token budget. When exact depth matching is infeasible, we use the closest feasible recursive configuration following prior recursive-sharing setups (Bae et al., 2025a; Bae et al., 2025b). Reported parameter counts denote unique trainable non-embedding parameters. All main decoder-only models use the same optimizer, learning-rate schedule, batch size, and hardware setup; full details are provided in Appendix A.

4.2 Main Results

We first compare BRT with static recursive sharing baselines using SmolLM-360M trained from scratch for 20B tokens. The baselines include Sequence and Cycle sharing, as well as Middle-Sequence and Middle-Cycle, where the first and last layers are kept independent of the recursive core. We evaluate two recursion settings, R=2R=2 and R=4R=4, which reduce the number of unique recurrent layers under matched or closest feasible executed depth. All models are evaluated on five benchmarks, and we report task-wise accuracy and average performance over three seeds. Detailed configurations and executed-depth accounting for all recursive variants are provided in Appendix A.

As shown in Table 1, BRT achieves the best average few-shot accuracy among static recursive sharing baselines under comparable or smaller unique-parameter budgets. With R=2R=2, BRT reaches 40.20 average accuracy, making it competitive with the vanilla model while using substantially fewer unique parameters. It also improves over Middle-Cycle, the strongest recursive baseline in this setting. With R=4R=4, BRT outperforms all recursive baselines and remains close to the vanilla model while using only 78M parameters. These results suggest that downstream performance depends not only on the number of shared parameters, but also on how reused layers are organized across depth.

4.3 Scaling with Compute and Data

Training Compute.

We evaluate language-modeling quality under different training compute budgets. Figure 3 reports validation negative log-likelihood (NLL) for SmolLM-360M variants with R=2R=2 and R=4R=4.

We compute NLL on 2,000 FineWeb-Edu validation samples and estimate training compute following Bae et al. (2025b), based on the scaling-law compute estimate of Kaplan et al. (2020). Across both recursion settings, BRT achieves the lowest validation NLL among static sharing strategies at all evaluated compute budgets. With R=2R=2, BRT improves over both Sequence and Cycle variants, showing that block-level reuse is beneficial even under moderate recursion. The gains are more pronounced with R=4R=4, where stronger compression leads to larger degradation for prior sharing variants. This trend is consistent with the view that global cyclic reuse can produce redundant updates, while overly fine-grained layer-wise reuse is also suboptimal. In contrast, BRT provides a more stable quality-compute trade-off by reusing intermediate contiguous blocks. Together with Table 1, these results show that BRT improves both downstream accuracy and validation NLL.

Matched Training Tokens.

We next evaluate how different sharing strategies scale with training tokens. Figure 4 reports mean accuracy over five benchmarks using SmolLM-135M and SmolLM-360M trained with 1B, 5B, 10B, and 20B tokens.

We evaluate both R=2R=2 and R=4R=4, and report mean performance over three seeds. For SmolLM-135M, vanilla models remain stronger than recursive variants in some low-data regimes, consistent with prior observations on small recursive models (Bae et al., 2025a; Bae et al., 2025b). However, BRT continues to benefit from additional training data and improves over the vanilla model at 20B tokens for both recursion settings. For SmolLM-360M, BRT outperforms static recursive baselines across token budgets and remains competitive with the vanilla model, especially under R=2R=2. Middle-Cycle also improves over Cycle at larger scale, suggesting that keeping the first and last layers independent is beneficial. Overall, these results suggest that block-level reuse becomes more stable as model size and training budget increase.

Billion-scale Architectures.

To test whether the gains of BRT extend beyond sub-billion models, we evaluate SmolLM-1.7B recursive architecture variants trained for 20B tokens. We compare BRT against Middle-Cycle, the strongest recursive baseline in our main experiments, and the vanilla model. We report task-wise and average performance across three seeds. In Table 2, BRT achieves 41.63 average accuracy, outperforming the Middle-Cycle variant with 41.33 average accuracy. It also remains competitive with the vanilla model, which achieves 41.68 average accuracy with approximately twice as many trainable parameters. The largest gain over Middle-Cycle appears on ARC, suggesting that block-level reuse can better preserve downstream performance in this setting. These results suggest that the benefits of BRT are not limited to sub-billion models and remain effective at billion-scale model sizes.

4.4 In-depth Analysis

We conduct ablation studies to analyze the effect of block granularity in BRT and to verify whether its gains come from the block-level reuse topology itself, rather than solely from adding boundary-independent layers. We pretrain SmolLM-360M from scratch on 10B tokens and evaluate all parameter-sharing variants on five few-shot benchmarks across three seeds. Table 3 provides the full task-wise results, while Figure 5 reports the average accuracy with the standard deviation values across seeds.

Block Granularity.

We first vary the number of blocks SS, while keeping the first and last layers independent. As shown in Table 3 and Figure 5, BRT achieves the best performance when S=2S=2, reaching 38.95 average accuracy and outperforming both the vanilla model and recursive sharing baselines. Increasing the number of blocks beyond this point does not further improve performance. Although S=3S=3 remains competitive with the vanilla model and outperforms Cycle sharing, S=4S=4 degrades downstream accuracy and even falls below the Cycle baseline. These results suggest that BRT benefits from an intermediate block granularity, where each recursive unit is large enough to coordinate local transformations but still avoids the overly global reuse imposed by Cycle sharing (S=1S=1).

Fully Recursive Setting.

We then remove the independent layers and force all layers to participate in the sharing strategy. This setting tests whether the advantage of BRT persists when the model becomes fully recursive. As shown in Table 3, BRT with S=2S=2 outperforms both Cycle sharing (S=1S=1) and Sequence sharing (S=16S=16), while remaining competitive with the vanilla model. This result is important because it shows that BRT can recover most of the vanilla model’s performance, unlike prior recursive sharing baselines.

In the fully recursive setting, we also observe that finer block partitions are not necessarily better. Increasing the number of blocks beyond two does not improve performance, following the same trend as when including the boundary-independent layers. As the block granularity becomes too fine, BRT approaches a structure similar to Sequence sharing and may inherit its limitations.

Overall, the S=2S=2 configuration provides the best balance between global reuse, as in Cycle sharing, and layer-level independent reuse, as in Sequence sharing. The fully recursive setting further shows that the gains of BRT cannot be explained solely by keeping the first and last layers independent. Although independent layers improve performance, block-level recursion remains stronger than prior sharing baselines even when all layers are recursively reused. These findings suggest that even with a smaller number of parameters and sometimes smaller executed depth, BRT provides a strong inductive bias for recursive Transformers.

4.5 Architecture Generalization

To examine whether the benefits of BRT extend beyond decoder-only architectures, we evaluate it on encoder-decoder and encoder-only Transformers. We use T5-220M for the encoder-decoder setting and ModernBERT-149M for the encoder-only setting (Raffel et al., 2020; Warner et al., 2025).

For each architecture, we compare BRT against the strongest Cycle and Sequence sharing variants, Middle-Cycle and Middle-Sequence. All models are pretrained from scratch on 10B tokens from FineWeb-Edu (Penedo et al., 2024), and we report the negative log-likelihood on the FineWeb-Edu validation set. Since T5 and ModernBERT differ in architecture and training objective, we analyze them separately rather than comparing their absolute NLL values.

Encoder-decoder Architecture.

We first evaluate T5-220M. Since encoder-decoder models contain two Transformer stacks, we ablate where the recursive structure is applied. We consider three variants: applying recursion to both the encoder and decoder, only to the decoder, and only to the encoder. This allows us to analyze whether BRT is more effective in the bidirectional encoder, the autoregressive decoder, or their combination.

In Figure 6, BRT achieves the lowest negative log-likelihood in all three settings. When both encoder and decoder are recursive, BRT reduces NLL from 5.64 to 5.56. The same trend holds when only one stack is recursive, with the best NLL of 5.52 under decoder-only recursion. We hypothesize that tying the decoder’s cross-attention projection across recursions makes each decoder block act as an iterative source-conditioned refinement step.

Encoder-only Architecture.

We next evaluate an encoder-only architecture (ModernBERT-149M) to test whether the benefits of BRT also hold under a masked language modeling objective. Unlike T5, ModernBERT consists of a single bidirectional Transformer stack. In Figure 6, BRT achieves the lowest validation NLL among encoder-only variants, improving over both Middle-Sequence and Middle-Cycle. This result indicates that the advantage of BRT is not limited to autoregressive decoding or encoder-decoder attention. Even in a fully bidirectional encoder, organizing parameter reuse into blocks provides a more effective recursive structure than either repeating individual layers or cycling through the entire stack.

Overall, these results suggest that block-level reuse is not specific to decoder-only models. Across encoder-decoder and encoder-only architectures, BRT consistently improves over prior static sharing baselines, supporting block granularity and reuse topology as important design factors for recursive Transformers.

5 Conclusion

We introduced Block Recursive Transformers (BRT), a static recursive sharing architecture that treats reuse topology as a key design factor. The proposed method partitions layers into contiguous blocks and recursively reuses each block before transitioning to the next, providing an intermediate topology between layer-wise repetition and global cyclic reuse. Across model scales, data budgets, recursion settings, and architecture types, BRT improves validation negative log-likelihood and downstream accuracy over static recursive sharing baselines. Ablations and representation analyses further show that intermediate block granularity better balances local refinement and depth-wise differentiation. More broadly, our findings suggest that the Recursive Transformer community should consider not only how much sharing is used, but also how reuse is organized across depth.

Limitations

Our analysis uses a fixed block partition to study block-level recursion in a controlled setting. We do not examine flexible partitioning strategies, such as asymmetric block designs or learned block partitioning. Investigating adaptive block structures across model scales and architectures is a future direction. In addition, our task coverage is limited to five few-shot evaluation benchmarks. Evaluating BRT on broader tasks, including multilingual settings, coding, and complex reasoning, is another future direction.

Appendix

This appendix provides additional implementation details and supporting analyses for the experiments included in the main paper. We include the model configurations used across architectures, describe the training and evaluation settings, and specify how executed depth and parameter counts are computed for each sharing strategy. We also provide additional visualization results to complement the CKA analysis of the main paper, and include the training dynamics of different sharing strategies. We organize these points as follows:

  • •

    Appendix A provides the full experimental setup for the experiments across decoder-only, encoder-only and encoder-decoder architectures, details of the different configurations for the parameter-sharing strategies, and explains how depth is computed for BRT.

  • •

    Appendix B extends the CKA visualizations from the main body, including a layer-by-layer visualization of the vanilla and Sequence-sharing strategy, and includes training-dynamic visualizations for BRT, Middle-Cycle and Middle-Sequence.

Appendix A Implementation Details

Table 4 summarizes the five base model configurations used in our experiments. These models cover the three Transformer architecture families considered in this work: decoder-only, encoder-decoder, and encoder-only architectures. For each model we report the original parameter count and executed depth before applying the different recursive parameter sharing strategies. We describe their training setup in the following subsections.

Decoder-only experiments.

For our main experiments, we use a LLaMA-based (Touvron et al., 2023) SmolLM architecture (Allal et al., 2024). We evaluate the 135M, 360M, and 1.7B variants to compare parameter-sharing strategies across model scales. Unless otherwise specified, all models are pretrained from scratch on a subset of the FineWeb-Edu dataset (Penedo et al., 2024) for up to 20B tokens, depending on the experimental setting. For BRT, we use S=2S=2 blocks by default.

For training, we use 8 NVIDIA A6000 GPUs with a total batch size of 1024. We use AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) as the optimizer with β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9 and β2=0.95\beta_{2}=0.95, and set the peak learning rate to 3×10−33\times 10^{-3}. Training is performed using bfloat16 precision, and gradients are clipped to a maximum norm of 1.0. We use a trapezoidal learning rate schedule with a 5% warmup and 10% linear cooldown. We set the maximum input sequence length to 2048.

We evaluate the models on five benchmarks from the Language Model Evaluation Harness (Sutawika et al., 2024): ARC, WinoGrande (WG), MMLU, HellaSwag (HS), and PIQA. We follow standard settings from prior work (Sakaguchi et al., 2021; Bisk et al., 2020; Clark et al., 2018; Zellers et al., 2019; Hendrycks et al., 2021), and evaluate using 5 shots for all benchmarks except ARC, where 25 shots are used. In addition, we also evaluate the models on the validation set of FineWeb-Edu and report the negative log-likelihood on 2,000 validation samples.

Encoder-decoder and encoder-only experiments.

For generalization purposes, we also conduct experiments on encoder-decoder and encoder-only architectures, using T5-220M and ModernBERT-149M, respectively (Raffel et al., 2020; Warner et al., 2025). In both settings, we train recursive variants from scratch for 10B tokens on the FineWeb-Edu dataset, and evaluate validation negative log-likelihood on 2,000 FineWeb-Edu samples (Penedo et al., 2024).

For both architectures, we use AdamW with β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9 and β2=0.95\beta_{2}=0.95, a total batch size of 1024, and 8 NVIDIA A6000 GPUs. Training is performed in bfloat16 precision, and gradients are clipped to a maximum norm of 0.5. We set the peak learning rate to 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} and use a trapezoidal learning-rate schedule with a 10% linear decay.

Unlike the decoder-only experiments, the encoder-decoder experiments use a span-corruption objective. For T5, we use a 20% warmup, relative position embeddings with maximum distance 1024 and 128 buckets, a decoder target length of 448, a noise density of 15%, and a mean span length of 3.1. We set the maximum input sequence length to 2048.

For the encoder-only experiments, we use a masked language modeling objective with a 15% masking rate. ModernBERT uses the same optimizer, peak learning rate, batch size, precision, gradient clipping and learning-rate schedule as the T5 experiments, except that the warmup is reduced to 10%. The maximum input sequence length is set to 1024.

Executed Depth and Total Parameters.

In Algorithm 1, we describe how we calculate executed depth for BRT. As indicated in Section 3, it is possible that the division operation is not feasible and that the depths do not match perfectly for all sharing strategies in all configurations. For BRT, we take this into account, and always select the closest depth value possible to the original vanilla depth. In particular, the depth of BRT will never be bigger than the vanilla depth, avoiding any kind of advantage over other baselines. For Sequence, Cycle, and their respective middle variants, we follow (Bae et al., 2025a; Bae et al., 2025b), where sharing strategies are allowed to have executed depths larger than those of the vanilla models. In Table 5 we report the non-embedding parameter count, executed depth, and number of unique layers across different sharing strategies for the different experiments.

Appendix B Extended Visualization Results

In Section 3, we motivated Block Recursive Transformers by the hierarchical functional roles that emerge across depth in Transformer models. Here, we extend our CKA analysis with additional heatmap visualizations to further examine these depth-wise patterns.

As shown in Figure 7, the vanilla Transformer exhibits a smooth evolution of representations across layers, with high similarity between adjacent layers and gradual transitions through depth. This suggests that depth naturally forms a small number of functionally coherent groups rather than a sequence of homogeneous transformations, consistent with our observation that partitioning layers into two blocks improves performance. In contrast, Sequence sharing shows uniformly high similarity across layers, including between early and late layers (Figure 8). This indicates limited depth-wise differentiation, aligning with the performance degradation observed for layer-wise sharing.

In addition, we visualize the behavior of global sharing in Figure 2. In this setting, all layers are grouped into a single shared function that is repeatedly applied. This design leads to highly redundant representations and limited evolution across recursion steps. One possible interpretation is that the model converges early to a fixed point, after which further recursions provide negligible additional computation. In contrast, BRT appears to better preserve the hierarchical structure of Transformers by exhibiting greater similarity among intra-block layers, with a smooth transition between layers, supporting depth specialization.

Training Dynamics.

Figure 9 shows the training dynamics of different sharing strategies using SmolLM-360M trained for 10B tokens. All methods follow a similar trajectory in the early stage of training, suggesting that the initial optimization is comparable across sharing strategies. However, after the initial billion tokens, BRT starts to separate from Middle-Cycle and Middle-Sequence, and achieves consistently lower training loss. This gap becomes more visible as training progresses, especially compared to Middle-Sequence. BRT achieves a training loss of 3.41 at 10B tokens, followed by Middle-Cycle and Middle-Sequence at 3.48 and 3.70, respectively.

We consider these results important because they show that the advantage of block-level reuse appears during training optimization, not only in final downstream performance. In this setting, BRT uses fewer parameters and smaller executed depth than the corresponding recursive baselines, so the lower training loss cannot be explained by additional capacity or computation. Instead, the results suggest that a better reuse organization could help optimize the training objective. This also supports the main empirical results obtained in the main paper: intermediate reuse granularity is a more effective sharing strategy relative to cycle and sequence sharing.

Overall, these results position intermediate block granularity as a key design factor for recursive Transformers.
